One meal a day

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
new diet advice -- eat only once a day.

Unique Selling Point:
Our viewers are extremely interested in diets and diets related stories.

Summary:
The diet revolution is far from over! Banting brought major changes in the way many people understand and consume food the world over. But that is just a good start! The revolution in understanding human diet takes another exciting new turn in a ground-breaking proposal by Dr. Marius Theron who takes the understanding of what an ideal diet is, a step further and argues that human beings are physiologically able to only eat once a day.

Further information:
REVOLUTIONARY NEW DIET
Low carb, high fat and most important of all – EAT ONLY ONCE A DAY.

The diet revolution is far from over! Banting brought major changes in the way many people understand and consume food the world over. But that is just a good start! The revolution in understanding human diet takes another exciting new turn in a ground-breaking proposal by Dr. Marius Theron who takes the understanding of what an ideal diet is, a step further and argues that human beings are physiologically programmed to only eat once a day.

“It brought me to the point of despair to see how people would diligently follow the wrong diet under the supervision of professionals. These diets were wrong in many ways. To this day it ingredients, timing and frequencies are totally unrelated to human anatomy and physiology design standards”, Marius writes. It is a sad fact that in medical schools only about 1-2% of of the curriculum is devoted to formal nutritional training, while in reality 60-80% of diagnoses are directly or indirectly related to diets gone wrong. The tsunami of modern chronic diseases can be linked directly to diet – obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer, dementia and a range of auto-immune diseases.

Marius Theron is a veterinarian and in his training he has enjoyed about 4 years of intensive nutritional education. “Or about 4 years more than I and my medical colleagues received in our undergraduate training”, says Prof Tim Noakes. This means that Marius with is veterinary background has a really thorough understanding of physiology and anatomy and how this relates to diet. Over the years he has come to the understanding that conventional teaching about nutrition is just simply wrong and not in alignment with what the human species actually requires.
His research started 20 years ago when he decided that, as modern humans are biologically closer to carnivores than to the primates from whom we evolved more directly, he should train himself to eat more like a carnivore than a large ape. So he began to mimic the way carnivores eat – a single large meal followed by a period of fasting until the urge to eat (or hunt) again. So today he eats 5-7 meals a week, comprising foods that provide 70% or more of his daily energy requirements from fat with less than 10% to 15% from carbohydrates.

In essence it means that he eats nutrient dense cooked foods once a day, usually at night. He little or no carbohydrate intake, but increased fat intake. According to conventional medical wisdom on diets that prescribes that at least 50-65% of our energy intake should come from carbohydrates and that it is advisable to eat at least 6 meals a day, his health should be a considerable risk. However, the opposite is true. Since turning to this diet he has experienced exceptional health and vitality. He has completed several ultra-distance events, including the run the Comrades marathon on this diet. “A detailed study of the coronary arteries supplying his heart muscle has shown that Marius Theron’s are not clogged with cholesterol. In fact, they are pristine”, writes Prof Tim Noakes in the foreword to the book.

It is a revolutionary way of viewing human diet, but it is based on solid science. This is necessary because Marius argues that there is no consensus among health fraternities what the correct diet is. “A loose-cannon mentality exists that empowers bureaucrats, pharmaceutical interests, insurance strategies, media popularity, food producers and merchants to dictate our diets standards.” He argues for introducing solid science into the equation and in his book has identified 5 secrets that have eluded nutritionists to a large extent, and they have to do with meal intervals, the timing of meals, the type of nutrients we should eat and the alignment of our metabolism to match this diet strategy. Each code in this book injects its own message about a healthy diet for humans, leaving no room for assumptions where proper science dictates otherwise.
Marius is supported in this programme by a number of experts, including Tim Noakes who has begun to follow the diet and now eats a single meal at intervals of 16-18 hours.

We have several case studies following the diet, including Noakes, a martial arts expert, athletes and ordinary people who all found it life-changing.

Marius Theron is willing to give us an exclusive on this, of we can do it fairly quickly.

Our viewers love diet-related stories and this one packs some punch because it propagates an eating strategy that is very unique, but back by considerable research.

ADDITIONAL INFO AFTER AMALIA COMMENTS

Hi Amalia,

The story is not a Banting story at all, nor is it about “intermittent daily fasting” (whatever that is).

From the beginning it was pitched as a one-meal-a-day lifestyle/diet, with the emphasis on one meal a day eating regime.

This guy and Tim Noakes did not know each other before he wrote the book late last year.

Marius Theron is a vet and thus has formal training in digestion, metabolism, etc. Not only of animals but also of humans. It is important to know this because he is not a crackpot making claims from nowhere without training.

Long before Noakes came up with reviving the Banting regime, Marius Theron concluded at a high fat low carb diet was ideal. He also noticed in his own life that he usually was not hungry early in the morning and slowly developed a lifestyle where he eats only in the evening. His research is based on basics of human physiology and metabolism such as the fact that sugar levels and insulin spike when we eat. This spike results in a cycle of energy storing in the body – as fat. As it passes your body goes into a cycle of energy utilization which burns fat. If you eat 7 times a day, it spikes every few hours and the cycle of energyfat utilization is interrupted and storage cycle starts up again. If you eat only once a day, the cycle is a short period of storing and a long period of energy utilization/fat burning where the calories taken in are utilised. He says it is very detrimental to have many sugar/insulin spikes per day.

In saying this he actually debunks a number of popular myths, and this is what I found interesting about the story:

Breakfast is the most important meal of the day. It was a slogan invented in 1944 to sell more cereal. Before cereal was invented, breakfast was a very secondary affair, if eaten at all. The cereals and breakfast food industry managed to turn breakfast into “the most important meal”. Incidentally, cereal was a product invented by John Harvey Kellogg, a deeply religious doctor who believed that cereal would both improve Americans' health and keep them from masturbating and desiring sex. (Only half of his message made it into the ads.)

Breakfast was always an important meal is a myth. In fact, throughout human history breakfast was mostly skipped. Even the Romans did not do breakfast. it seems that only after the industrial revolution breakfast was beginning to be taken by factory workers.

Don’t go to sleep on a full stomach is silly advice. Actually, for metabolism it is much better to eat the large meal in the evening. Eating a big breakfast is bad for you – a lot of blood flow is directed to the digestive system, resulting in less blood flow to peripheral parts of the body, even the brain (people get drowsy, inaccurate). This means people with a big breakfast actually function less effectively. Having a good meal at night and going to sleep makes more sense.

You need something to jump start your metabolism. There is no such thing. Your body don’t forget to function, it reacts to stimuli.

You need food at the beginning of the day for energy. You can consume enough calories in one meal to last you several days.
So the conclusion is that it is quite adequate and actually beneficial for humans to eat once a day and make that meal high fat and low carb, and eat it in the evening.

Marius started to follow this regime 17 years ago and along the way met surprisingly many people who also ate sparingly during the day. After comparing notes they all began to cut down to one meal a day, and found it meaningful. Then, based on his own experience and that of others, he decided to write the book and started a few years ago. Then the Banting thing came along which for him confirmed his high fat low carb diet. Last year he contacted Tim Noakes about it. Now Noakes is also following the diet.

Marius trained for the the Comrades and ran it on one meal a day and only on water. We can certainly check up on the veracity of this.

The case studies we have are:
Gerhard van der Westhuizen– a 61 year old who works out at least 3 hours a day, does mountain bike riding over weekends, etc. He is chosen because he is an example of an extremely fit, active person who only eats once a day.

Lucy Nel – a fifties-something woman who does not train at all. She was fat and had high cholesterol. She is now thin and her cholesterol under control. She has medical records to prove this.

Dean Jones – a martial artist who also trains very hard and follows the diet.

Tim Noakes

It goes without saying that we will also consult a traditional dietician. I was planning to use Bronwyn Stokes whom we had on the show previously and came across very well. In the proposal I only mention the case studies.

Press Release:


One Meal a Day
It’s a global obsession and controversial debate: what is the optimal diet required for human beings? How often and how much should we eat? Some say three square meals a day are ideal, others say six smaller meals are better. One school of thought that’s seemingly gaining traction says the answer is far simpler. Carte Blanche asks: are human beings biologically programmed to thrive on only a single meal a day?


Script:


V/O:
This is 60 year old Gerhard van Rensburg. He exercises for at least one and a half hours a day and cycles between 60 and 100 km every weekend. And he does this on only one meal a day which he eats at night.
Gerhard van Rensburg:
I wake up and I am not hungry, and I go through a day, and I am not hungry.
V/O:
Gerhard has been eating only once a day for several years now.
Gerhard:
If I don’t eat in the mornings I don't have to eat by lunchtime. Today, it is now 12 o'clock. I went to gym and I spent an hour and a half in the gym on a hard workout.
V/O:
He last ate last night and is only going to again eat later tonight.

Gerhard’s eating habits are based on a diet regime developed by Dr. Marius Theron from Pretoria. He had worked as a vet for 12 years before becoming involved in human nutrition and diets in the early 1990s. The he was confronted with the chaos surrounding dietary advice.
Marius Theron:
There were so many conflicts what people should eat, when they should eat, how much they should eat.

Devi:
Even now. Every year there seems to be a new rule. Or a new idea

Marius:
A new idea, a novel idea. And it is about to become the most popular on the block for a while. And then it would disappear and be replaced by something else.
V/O:
He found this perplexing bcause as a vet he had received four years of intensive training on a variety of animal digestive systems. For him the solution was fairly simple: humans should eat like the animals he says we are closest to – carnivores.
V/O:
Professor Tim Noakes, well known for his research on diet and nutrition, agrees that humans can primarily be classified as meat-eaters.
Tim:
We are absolutely carnivores, if you look from our teeth to our gut. We are carnivores, we are out and out carnivores.
V/O:
A carnivorous diet consists mainly of animal protein and fat. And they do not have obesity problems.
Devi:
I have never seen a fat carnivore.
Tim:
No you never will

Devi:
But they will do more exercise...

Tim:
You will see them in parks because they feed carbohydrates and you will see them, dogs and cats. There is an epidemic of domestic cats and dogs with obesity, diabetes and cancer. Surprise! Feed carnivores carbohydrates and they develop cancer.
V/O:
Humans develop the same diseases. Marius suggests that if humans were to adapt their diet to be more in line with the way carnivores eat in nature, not only would they be lean, but healthier as well.

So, 18 years ago he started to emulate a carnivorous diet: eating less frequently and eating fat and protein rich food with few carbohydrates. He called it a wolf diet.
Marius:
The philosophy behind this Wolf diet is to become a carnivore. To be the animal you are supposed to be.
V/O:
Thando Mabusa, a registered dietician is very sceptical about this kind of diet.
Thando:
I don’t think humans are carnivores, clearly because we have so much other enzymes to break down other food groups. There are so many vitamins and minerals that we get from other food that we can’t get from meat, that we get from other food groups.
V/O:
In fact, Thando says what Marius proposes is diametrically opposed to current views on human diet.
Thando:
We dieticians promote a high fibre low fat diet for healthy individuals. Breakfast is an important meal. We think it is good, healthy to have three main meals and three snacks. A big meal at night is not recommended
V/O:
But Marius says current dietary advice actually promotes obesity – linked to the consumption of carbohydrates. When we eat carbohydrates, our blood sugar levels spike and our body reacts by releasing insulin to counter this.
Tim:
Insulin is the fat building hormone. It drives the fat into the fat cells but it also prevents it coming out. So the moment you raise your insulin, the only fuels you can burn is carbohydrates. You can't get to those fat cells

Devi:
The fat gets locked into the cells...

Tim:
The fat gets locked into the cells.
V/O:
And this is the reason why people get fat on a diet rich in carbohydrates – their insulin levels are con/tin/uously high, more fat is forced into fat cells and the stored fat remains locked in and cannot be utilized by the body.
Tim:
So the moment you get your insulin down, then the fat is readily available to be burned.
V/O:
And one way to keep insulin levels down is by eating less frequently, says Marius.
Marius:
Carnivores would tend to eat 3 times a week

Devi:
So you started having one meal a day?

Marius:
Yes. So that is 7 times a week I would eat, obviously one meal a day. On the fact that I can eat one day's energy in one meal. One sit-down, three course meal would easily supply you with 3 days’ worth of energy.
V/O:
Tim agrees and says it was only fairly recently that people started to eat several times a day.
Tim:
Humans are designed to eat once, maybe twice a day. And if you go back to when we used to be hunter gatherers, you would kill food once every few days. And that is our biology is designed for a metabolism that is infrequent. We are not designed to eat frequently. If you eat real food with a lot of fat and a lot of protein, you can eat once or twice a day because you don’t become hungry.
V/O
This is exactly what Gerhard experiences, despite eating only every 24 hours and working out hard.

Gerhard:
I don’t get hungry. I don’t become hungry.

Lucy Nel also follows this diet. She has lost a lot of weight on it and doesn’t find it difficult to follow.
Devi:
The point is you are not hungry at any stage?

Lucy:
No, I think that to me was probably the greatest achievement in my life. But when I became aware that I am no longer hungry, I can walk past any restaurant. You can still smell it but you don’t feel the hunger.
V/O:
Lucy says this diet has changed her life and health completely.
Lucy & Devi:
So now I actually eat what I love eating and I do it once a day and at night time.

Devi:
How do you feel?

Lucy:
I feel brilliant. I feel healthy, I feel energetic. I feel good.
V/O:
Eating once a day directly contradicts traditional advice to eat several times during the day.
Marius:
That is so wrong. Anybody that understands metabolism on the basis of first year physiology would tell you that that is absolutely a misconception, completely.
V/O:
Marius says when we eat a meal, our insulin level spikes, but returns to a low very quickly, opening the way for stored fat to be utilized. So, if you eat once every 24 hours there is a long period over which your body gets a chance to utilize the stored fat for energy, and you slim down.

If you eat many times a day, your blood sugar and insulin levels spike every few hours, and this prevents any of the stored fat from being released. This is one of the reasons why there is such an obesity epidemic worldwide.

In addition, a conTin/uously spiking blood sugar and insulin level is very detrimental to health in the long term.
Tim:
And it is these repetitive spikes of glucose and insulin every three hours that cause damage. Because we have pancreas that secrete the insulin and eventually it gets tired and can’t secrete the insulin and then we become frankly diabetic. But every time you secrete insulin.... insulin is an aging hormone it damages your arteries. The longer we can delay eating, the better your health would be in the long term.
Marius:
People who eat once a day, a high fat diet, they do not become diabetics. You cannot become a diabetic by eating once a day. It is impossible.
V/O:
Another cornerstone of Marius’ wolf diet is that he eats his only meal of the day in the evening.
Marius:
Is it safer to walk around digesting a huge breakfast or go to bed sleeping on a big dinner? It is safer to sleep with a full stomach than walking around with a full stomach. It interferes on your focus and concentration.
V/O:
So for Marius it makes sense to eat in the evening. And this is what he had for dinner last Thursday night. Two eggs, a slice of bread, half an avo with cream cheese, chicken livers slow cooked with lots of butter and some chakalaka for flavour. He says it’s enough to last him 24 hours.

And by skipping breakfast, he challenges another dietary myth.
LINK
Conventional wisdom dictates that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. But few people realise that is a recent invention.
V/O:
In fact, the slogan is from a 1944 marketing campaign to promote breakfast cereal. And throughout human history breakfast was seldom eaten.

Marius says this is because one meal high in fat and protein provides enough energy to last 24 hours.
LINK:
The belief is that you can not only survive but even serious sportsmen can thrive on one meal a day.
V/O:
Marius himself has run the Comrades -- 89 kilometres on no food and just water.
Gerhard similarly exercises hard every day – and thrives on just one meal a day.
V/O:
Marius felt so strongly about his carnivore diet that he wrote a book about it called the “Secrets of the Diet Codes” in which he explains the diet and the biology behind it.

However, Thando is convinced that the fasting associated with one meal a day is not healthy.
Thando:
Your glucose levels are constantly low. Fasting in the long term is not feasible at all. You can't live off starving. And having one meal is just not sufficient to supply your body with enough nutrients and vitamins needed.
V/O:
Tim who eats one meal and a snack per day is positive about Marius’ diet regime.
Tim:
There is absolutely no evidence that anything he says is damaging to our health or does not apply to all of us. My point would be that we are designed to eat much less frequently than we do.

How often and how much should we eat? Some say three square meals a day are ideal, others say six smaller meals are better. One school of thought that’s seemingly gaining traction says the answer is far simpler. Carte Blanche asks: are human beings biologically programmed to thrive on only a single meal a day? Script: V/O: This is 60 year old Gerhard van Rensburg. He exercises for at least one and a half hours a day and cycles between 60 and 100 km every weekend. And he does this on only one meal a day which he eats at night. Gerhard van Rensburg: I wake up and I am not hungry, and I go through a day, and I am not hungry. V/O: Gerhard has been eating only once a day for several years now. Gerhard: If I don’t eat in the mornings I don't have to eat by lunchtime. Today, it is now 12 o'clock. I went to gym and I spent an hour and a half in the gym on a hard workout. V/O: He last ate last night and is only going to again eat later tonight. Gerhard’s eating habits are based on a diet regime developed by Dr. Marius Theron from Pretoria. He had worked as a vet for 12 years before becoming involved in human nutrition and diets in the early 1990s. The he was confronted with the chaos surrounding dietary advice. Marius Theron: There were so many conflicts what people should eat, when they should eat, how much they should eat. Devi: Even now. Every year there seems to be a new rule. Or a new idea Marius: A new idea, a novel idea. And it is about to become the most popular on the block for a while. And then it would disappear and be replaced by something else. V/O: He found this perplexing bcause as a vet he had received four years of intensive training on a variety of animal digestive systems. For him the solution was fairly simple: humans should eat like the animals he says we are closest to – carnivores. V/O: Professor Tim Noakes, well known for his research on diet and nutrition, agrees that humans can primarily be classified as meat-eaters. Tim: We are absolutely carnivores, if you look from our teeth to our gut. We are carnivores, we are out and out carnivores. V/O: A carnivorous diet consists mainly of animal protein and fat. And they do not have obesity problems. Devi: I have never seen a fat carnivore. Tim: No you never will Devi: But they will do more exercise... Tim: You will see them in parks because they feed carbohydrates and you will see them, dogs and cats. There is an epidemic of domestic cats and dogs with obesity, diabetes and cancer. Surprise! Feed carnivores carbohydrates and they develop cancer. V/O: Humans develop the same diseases. Marius suggests that if humans were to adapt their diet to be more in line with the way carnivores eat in nature, not only would they be lean, but healthier as well. So, 18 years ago he started to emulate a carnivorous diet: eating less frequently and eating fat and protein rich food with few carbohydrates. He called it a wolf diet. Marius: The philosophy behind this Wolf diet is to become a carnivore. To be the animal you are supposed to be. V/O: Thando Mabusa, a registered dietician is very sceptical about this kind of diet. Thando: I don’t think humans are carnivores, clearly because we have so much other enzymes to break down other food groups. There are so many vitamins and minerals that we get from other food that we can’t get from meat, that we get from other food groups. V/O: In fact, Thando says what Marius proposes is diametrically opposed to current views on human diet. Thando: We dieticians promote a high fibre low fat diet for healthy individuals. Breakfast is an important meal. We think it is good, healthy to have three main meals and three snacks. A big meal at night is not recommended V/O: But Marius says current dietary advice actually promotes obesity – linked to the consumption of carbohydrates. When we eat carbohydrates, our blood sugar levels spike and our body reacts by releasing insulin to counter this. Tim: Insulin is the fat building hormone. It drives the fat into the fat cells but it also prevents it coming out. So the moment you raise your insulin, the only fuels you can burn is carbohydrates. You can't get to those fat cells Devi: The fat gets locked into the cells... Tim: The fat gets locked into the cells. V/O: And this is the reason why people get fat on a diet rich in carbohydrates – their insulin levels are con/tin/uously high, more fat is forced into fat cells and the stored fat remains locked in and cannot be utilized by the body. Tim: So the moment you get your insulin down, then the fat is readily available to be burned. V/O: And one way to keep insulin levels down is by eating less frequently, says Marius. Marius: Carnivores would tend to eat 3 times a week Devi: So you started having one meal a day? Marius: Yes. So that is 7 times a week I would eat, obviously one meal a day. On the fact that I can eat one day's energy in one meal. One sit-down, three course meal would easily supply you with 3 days’ worth of energy. V/O: Tim agrees and says it was only fairly recently that people started to eat several times a day. Tim: Humans are designed to eat once, maybe twice a day. And if you go back to when we used to be hunter gatherers, you would kill food once every few days. And that is our biology is designed for a metabolism that is infrequent. We are not designed to eat frequently. If you eat real food with a lot of fat and a lot of protein, you can eat once or twice a day because you don’t become hungry. V/O This is exactly what Gerhard experiences, despite eating only every 24 hours and working out hard. Gerhard: I don’t get hungry. I don’t become hungry. Lucy Nel also follows this diet. She has lost a lot of weight on it and doesn’t find it difficult to follow. Devi: The point is you are not hungry at any stage? Lucy: No, I think that to me was probably the greatest achievement in my life. But when I became aware that I am no longer hungry, I can walk past any restaurant. You can still smell it but you don’t feel the hunger. V/O: Lucy says this diet has changed her life and health completely. Lucy & Devi: So now I actually eat what I love eating and I do it once a day and at night time. Devi: How do you feel? Lucy: I feel brilliant. I feel healthy, I feel energetic. I feel good. V/O: Eating once a day directly contradicts traditional advice to eat several times during the day. Marius: That is so wrong. Anybody that understands metabolism on the basis of first year physiology would tell you that that is absolutely a misconception, completely. V/O: Marius says when we eat a meal, our insulin level spikes, but returns to a low very quickly, opening the way for stored fat to be utilized. So, if you eat once every 24 hours there is a long period over which your body gets a chance to utilize the stored fat for energy, and you slim down. If you eat many times a day, your blood sugar and insulin levels spike every few hours, and this prevents any of the stored fat from being released. This is one of the reasons why there is such an obesity epidemic worldwide. In addition, a conTin/uously spiking blood sugar and insulin level is very detrimental to health in the long term. Tim: And it is these repetitive spikes of glucose and insulin every three hours that cause damage. Because we have pancreas that secrete the insulin and eventually it gets tired and can’t secrete the insulin and then we become frankly diabetic. But every time you secrete insulin.... insulin is an aging hormone it damages your arteries. The longer we can delay eating, the better your health would be in the long term. Marius: People who eat once a day, a high fat diet, they do not become diabetics. You cannot become a diabetic by eating once a day. It is impossible. V/O: Another cornerstone of Marius’ wolf diet is that he eats his only meal of the day in the evening. Marius: Is it safer to walk around digesting a huge breakfast or go to bed sleeping on a big dinner? It is safer to sleep with a full stomach than walking around with a full stomach. It interferes on your focus and concentration. V/O: So for Marius it makes sense to eat in the evening. And this is what he had for dinner last Thursday night. Two eggs, a slice of bread, half an avo with cream cheese, chicken livers slow cooked with lots of butter and some chakalaka for flavour. He says it’s enough to last him 24 hours. And by skipping breakfast, he challenges another dietary myth. LINK Conventional wisdom dictates that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. But few people realise that is a recent invention. V/O: In fact, the slogan is from a 1944 marketing campaign to promote breakfast cereal. And throughout human history breakfast was seldom eaten. Marius says this is because one meal high in fat and protein provides enough energy to last 24 hours. LINK: The belief is that you can not only survive but even serious sportsmen can thrive on one meal a day. V/O: Marius himself has run the Comrades -- 89 kilometres on no food and just water. Gerhard similarly exercises hard every day – and thrives on just one meal a day. V/O: Marius felt so strongly about his carnivore diet that he wrote a book about it called the “Secrets of the Diet Codes” in which he explains the diet and the biology behind it. However, Thando is convinced that the fasting associated with one meal a day is not healthy. Thando: Your glucose levels are constantly low. Fasting in the long term is not feasible at all. You can't live off starving. And having one meal is just not sufficient to supply your body with enough nutrients and vitamins needed. V/O: Tim who eats one meal and a snack per day is positive about Marius’ diet regime. Tim: There is absolutely no evidence that anything he says is damaging to our health or does not apply to all of us. My point would be that we are designed to eat much less frequently than we do.

metadata.Further information: REVOLUTIONARY NEW DIET Low carb, high fat and most important of all – EAT ONLY ONCE A DAY. The diet revolution is far from over! Banting brought major changes in the way many people understand and consume food the world over. But that is just a good start! The revolution in understanding human diet takes another exciting new turn in a ground-breaking proposal by Dr. Marius Theron who takes the understanding of what an ideal diet is, a step further and argues that human beings are physiologically programmed to only eat once a day. “It brought me to the point of despair to see how people would diligently follow the wrong diet under the supervision of professionals. These diets were wrong in many ways. To this day it ingredients, timing and frequencies are totally unrelated to human anatomy and physiology design standards”, Marius writes. It is a sad fact that in medical schools only about 1-2% of of the curriculum is devoted to formal nutritional training, while in reality 60-80% of diagnoses are directly or indirectly related to diets gone wrong. The tsunami of modern chronic diseases can be linked directly to diet – obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer, dementia and a range of auto-immune diseases. Marius Theron is a veterinarian and in his training he has enjoyed about 4 years of intensive nutritional education. “Or about 4 years more than I and my medical colleagues received in our undergraduate training”, says Prof Tim Noakes. This means that Marius with is veterinary background has a really thorough understanding of physiology and anatomy and how this relates to diet. Over the years he has come to the understanding that conventional teaching about nutrition is just simply wrong and not in alignment with what the human species actually requires. His research started 20 years ago when he decided that, as modern humans are biologically closer to carnivores than to the primates from whom we evolved more directly, he should train himself to eat more like a carnivore than a large ape. So he began to mimic the way carnivores eat – a single large meal followed by a period of fasting until the urge to eat (or hunt) again. So today he eats 5-7 meals a week, comprising foods that provide 70% or more of his daily energy requirements from fat with less than 10% to 15% from carbohydrates. In essence it means that he eats nutrient dense cooked foods once a day, usually at night. He little or no carbohydrate intake, but increased fat intake. According to conventional medical wisdom on diets that prescribes that at least 50-65% of our energy intake should come from carbohydrates and that it is advisable to eat at least 6 meals a day, his health should be a considerable risk. However, the opposite is true. Since turning to this diet he has experienced exceptional health and vitality. He has completed several ultra-distance events, including the run the Comrades marathon on this diet. “A detailed study of the coronary arteries supplying his heart muscle has shown that Marius Theron’s are not clogged with cholesterol. In fact, they are pristine”, writes Prof Tim Noakes in the foreword to the book. It is a revolutionary way of viewing human diet, but it is based on solid science. This is necessary because Marius argues that there is no consensus among health fraternities what the correct diet is. “A loose-cannon mentality exists that empowers bureaucrats, pharmaceutical interests, insurance strategies, media popularity, food producers and merchants to dictate our diets standards.” He argues for introducing solid science into the equation and in his book has identified 5 secrets that have eluded nutritionists to a large extent, and they have to do with meal intervals, the timing of meals, the type of nutrients we should eat and the alignment of our metabolism to match this diet strategy. Each code in this book injects its own message about a healthy diet for humans, leaving no room for assumptions where proper science dictates otherwise. Marius is supported in this programme by a number of experts, including Tim Noakes who has begun to follow the diet and now eats a single meal at intervals of 16-18 hours. We have several case studies following the diet, including Noakes, a martial arts expert, athletes and ordinary people who all found it life-changing. Marius Theron is willing to give us an exclusive on this, of we can do it fairly quickly. Our viewers love diet-related stories and this one packs some punch because it propagates an eating strategy that is very unique, but back by considerable research. ADDITIONAL INFO AFTER AMALIA COMMENTS Hi Amalia, The story is not a Banting story at all, nor is it about “intermittent daily fasting” (whatever that is). From the beginning it was pitched as a one-meal-a-day lifestyle/diet, with the emphasis on one meal a day eating regime. This guy and Tim Noakes did not know each other before he wrote the book late last year. Marius Theron is a vet and thus has formal training in digestion, metabolism, etc. Not only of animals but also of humans. It is important to know this because he is not a crackpot making claims from nowhere without training. Long before Noakes came up with reviving the Banting regime, Marius Theron concluded at a high fat low carb diet was ideal. He also noticed in his own life that he usually was not hungry early in the morning and slowly developed a lifestyle where he eats only in the evening. His research is based on basics of human physiology and metabolism such as the fact that sugar levels and insulin spike when we eat. This spike results in a cycle of energy storing in the body – as fat. As it passes your body goes into a cycle of energy utilization which burns fat. If you eat 7 times a day, it spikes every few hours and the cycle of energyfat utilization is interrupted and storage cycle starts up again. If you eat only once a day, the cycle is a short period of storing and a long period of energy utilization/fat burning where the calories taken in are utilised. He says it is very detrimental to have many sugar/insulin spikes per day. In saying this he actually debunks a number of popular myths, and this is what I found interesting about the story: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day. It was a slogan invented in 1944 to sell more cereal. Before cereal was invented, breakfast was a very secondary affair, if eaten at all. The cereals and breakfast food industry managed to turn breakfast into “the most important meal”. Incidentally, cereal was a product invented by John Harvey Kellogg, a deeply religious doctor who believed that cereal would both improve Americans' health and keep them from masturbating and desiring sex. (Only half of his message made it into the ads.) Breakfast was always an important meal is a myth. In fact, throughout human history breakfast was mostly skipped. Even the Romans did not do breakfast. it seems that only after the industrial revolution breakfast was beginning to be taken by factory workers. Don’t go to sleep on a full stomach is silly advice. Actually, for metabolism it is much better to eat the large meal in the evening. Eating a big breakfast is bad for you – a lot of blood flow is directed to the digestive system, resulting in less blood flow to peripheral parts of the body, even the brain (people get drowsy, inaccurate). This means people with a big breakfast actually function less effectively. Having a good meal at night and going to sleep makes more sense. You need something to jump start your metabolism. There is no such thing. Your body don’t forget to function, it reacts to stimuli. You need food at the beginning of the day for energy. You can consume enough calories in one meal to last you several days. So the conclusion is that it is quite adequate and actually beneficial for humans to eat once a day and make that meal high fat and low carb, and eat it in the evening. Marius started to follow this regime 17 years ago and along the way met surprisingly many people who also ate sparingly during the day. After comparing notes they all began to cut down to one meal a day, and found it meaningful. Then, based on his own experience and that of others, he decided to write the book and started a few years ago. Then the Banting thing came along which for him confirmed his high fat low carb diet. Last year he contacted Tim Noakes about it. Now Noakes is also following the diet. Marius trained for the the Comrades and ran it on one meal a day and only on water. We can certainly check up on the veracity of this. The case studies we have are: Gerhard van der Westhuizen– a 61 year old who works out at least 3 hours a day, does mountain bike riding over weekends, etc. He is chosen because he is an example of an extremely fit, active person who only eats once a day. Lucy Nel – a fifties-something woman who does not train at all. She was fat and had high cholesterol. She is now thin and her cholesterol under control. She has medical records to prove this. Dean Jones – a martial artist who also trains very hard and follows the diet. Tim Noakes It goes without saying that we will also consult a traditional dietician. I was planning to use Bronwyn Stokes whom we had on the show previously and came across very well. In the proposal I only mention the case studies.
